Mudgalapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् contain a lot of ancient historical traditions and material though couched in the style and language of म्य्थोलोग्य्.
Generally, they are divided into two groups: Mahāpurāṇas (the major पुराणस्) and उपपुराणस् (the minor पुराणस्). The Mudgalapurāṇa is one classed among the latter group of works.
Written probably during the period A. D. 900-1100, it is devoted mainly to the description of nine incarnations of गणपति. They are: Vakratuṇḍa, एकदन्त, Mahodara, Gajānana, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnarāja, Dhūmravarṇa and योग.
It speaks of 23 more forms of गणपति. It has imbibed the influence of the तन्त्रस् very much.
See also PURĀṆAS.

mudrā
(‘that which gives pleasure [to the deity]’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘mudrā’ has been used in several senses. Etymologically, it means ‘that which gives pleasure to the deity and makes its heart melt out of compassion’.
In the आगमस् and तन्त्रस्, it is used to indicate: a pose of hand; a posture of the body; as one of the five makāras (various kinds of grains); a woman companion of the tāntrik sādhaka.
In dance also several mudrās indicating several bhāvas or sentiments are used.
In iconographical works, the images are depicted as exhibiting several mudrās (poses of hand) like abhayamudrā (pose of protection) or varadamudrā (pose of granting boons) or चिन्मुद्रा (pose of imparting knowledge).
In pūja or worship, some of the mudrās (poses) used are āvāhanī (inviting the deity) or sammukhīkaraṇī (requesting the deity to turn towards the worshipper), कूर्म (in meditation on the deity) and avaguṇṭhana (covering the ड़ोओद् ceremonially while offering it).
The mudrās (also called bandhas) in हठयोग vary from 8 to 108. They indicate several processes of controlling the body and the prāṇic energy which give health, strength and energy as also freedom from diseases. Some of these mudrās are: mahāmudrā, nabhomudrā, mātāṅginī and so on.
In the political sciences as depicted in the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (321-300 B. C.), a मुद्रा represents a seal of the government. Different kinds of seals were used for different purposes like seals on merchandise for having paid the tax or about their quality or while issuing instructions in the name of the king.
Sometimes, those who committed abominable crimes were branded with certain signs called ‘mudrās’ and banished from the kingdom. For instance, a thief was branded with the sign of a dog on his forehead.
See also BANDHA, PŪJĀ and TANTRAS.

Mudgala Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् assigned to the Ṛgveda. It is like a brief commentary on the Puruṣasūkta (vide Ṛgveda 10.7.90.1-16). There are four khaṇḍas or sections with 30 mantras in all. Only the first section is in verses in the anuṣṭubh metre. The rest are in prose.
The first section gives a brief explanation of the various verses of the Puruṣa-sūkta. For instance, the word ‘sahasra śīrṣā’ (verse 1) indicates that the पुरुष (God) is infinite. The second verse describes him as the giver of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. The verses 16 and 17 describe the greatness of Hari (= पुरुष).
The second section says that भगवान् वासुदेव gave this teaching of the Puruṣasūkta to इन्द्र, the king of gods. नारायण, the Paramapuruṣa (the Supreme Person), though beyond names and forms and ordinary knowledge, assumed this form of the thousand-headed पुरुष for the benefit of ordinary mortals, so that they could attain लिबेरतिओन् just by looking at him. It was this Puruṣa—called ‘Mahāpuruṣa’ here—that divided himself into four forms, out of which only one is here manifested as this world, the rest being beyond च्रेअतिओन् and comprehension.
It is him—who has manifested himself in various forms—that the अध्वर्यु priests worship as the threefold अग्नि (fire-god). It is again him that others identify with the three वेदस्. Others again—like human beings, demons and manes—identify him with rayi (food), delusive power or with the मन्त्र ‘svadhā’ used in sacrifices. This is the gist of the third section.
The last section describes that ब्रह्मन् (= पुरुष) is without the six kośas or sheaths like skin and blood, beyond the six ūrmis or infirmities like hunger and thirst as also the six bhāvas or changes like birth and death. But the Supreme पुरुष somehow, voluntarily, accepts these and becomes the जीव (individual सोउल् in bondage).
One who studies this Upaniṣad becomes pure in every way. He is liberated from all sins of all types. However, being an esoteric knowledge of the highest, it should never be imparted to unworthy persons who have not studied the वेदस् or who have not performed sacrifices or who are harsh of speech and ever discontented.
The गुरु who gives this knowledge to worthy disciples must follow some sacred rules like choosing a clean place, an auspicious time and meditation on the पुरुष. He should impart it secretly in the ear of the disciple.
Then, both the teacher and the disciple become identified with the पुरुष himself.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Mudgala
------------------------------------------
Mudgala was a great sage performing austerities at कुरुक्षेत्र. He was the ड़थेर् of दिवोदास (a king) and अहल्या (the wife of the sage गौतम). He was well-known for his होस्पितलित्य् to guests. He once rejected the offer of the gods to go to हेअवेन् since he was interested in मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
He is said to have performed a great sacrifice near the bridge built by Śrī राम. Pleased with it Lord विष्णु created a big pond of milk (of कामधेनु, the celestial cow) to be used in his sacrifice. This pond called Kṣīratīrtha which is near Rāmeś-varam is visited by the pilgrims even now.
Mudgala is the sage of the Ṛgvedic सूक्त 10.102. It is mentioned there that his cows were once stolen. He yoked an old ox to his cart, followed the thieves and got back his cows after routing them with his drughaṇa (wooden mace). His wife, Mudgalānī drove his cart or chariot, thus helping him in this venture.

Muddusvāmi Dīkṣitar
(A. D. 1775-1835)
------------------------------------------
The science of Hindu मुसिच्, though originally one, gradually got crystallised into two broad traditions: The uttarādi (North Indian) and the dakṣiṇādi (South Indian, also called Karnatic).
If the saint Purandara Dāsa (A. D. 1484-1564) laid the foundation for the present form of South Indian मुसिच्, the three jewels (‘ratnatraya’) of the same system have enriched it abundantly. They are: त्यागराज (A. D. 1767-1847), Muddu-svāmi Dīkṣitar (A. D. 1775-1835) and श्यामाशास्त्रि (A. D. 1763-1827).
Muddusvāmi Dīkṣitar—also known as Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar or just ‘Dīkṣitar’—was the son of Rāmasvāmi Dīkṣitar and Subbalakṣmi Ammāḷ, born as a result of the grace of the Divine मोथेर् Bālāmbikā (Pārvatī) (of Vaidīśvaran Koil, a famous temple in Tamil Nadu). This is obviously reflected in many of the compositions of Dīkṣitar on the मोथेर् Divine.
Muddusvāmi—known in his earlier days as Kumārasvāmi—was the eldest son and had three younger brothers. He was well-educated by his ड़थेर् himself in several branches of knowledge like the वेदस्, सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे and literary works, health sciences, mantraśāstra (esoteric science of sacred formulae) and मुसिच्. Cidambaranātha, a great योगि, who was the गुरु of Rāmasvāmi Dīkṣitar, took him and Muddusvāmi to काशी where they spent six years. During this sojourn in the north, the boy not only visited many places of पिल्ग्रिमगे but also picked up a fairly good knowledge of the North Indian मुसिच्. Its influence can be noticed in some of his compositions like ‘raṅgapuravihara,’ ‘jambūpate māṁ pāhi,’ and ‘akhilāṇ-ḍeśvari.’
Muddusvāmi Dīkṣitar then returned to his native place Maṇali.
Once he went to Tiruttaṇi, a nearby sacred place and practised special spiritual disciplines, meditating on the deity सुब्रह्मण्य. A strange mystical experience here induced in him a remarkable power to compose songs. This is the reason why his songs always contain the words ‘Guruguha’ (= सुब्रह्मण्य) towards the end.
Later in life he toured South India extensively and composed songs on the various deities of the Hindu pantheon (the presiding deities of the places visited).
He had met both त्यागराज and श्यामाशास्त्रि in his tours.
Dīkṣitar was not only a composer and singer but also an accomplished player of vīṇā (lute).
All his compositions are in Sanskrit and excel not only in diction but also in rousing our devotion. His ‘navāvaraṇa-kṛtis’ are special compositions on the esoteric worship of the Divine मोथेर्.
He intuitively perceived that his death was very near and passed away when his disciples were singing—at his behest—his famous song ‘mīnākṣi me mudaṁ dehi’.
He left behind him a galaxy of disciples to continue his tradition.
